```{r fig-top5-odor-un-family, fig.cap = "Figure 14d. Five lowest-p taxa at Family level (ANCOM-BC2), Unpleasant vs Normal."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_fecal_odor_U_vs_Normal_family.png"))
```

* **Robust, higher in Unpleasant:** `r rob(anc_un, "Family")`.
* **Robust, higher in Normal:** `r rob(anc_un, "Family", up = FALSE)`; these two
  Coriobacteriales families nearly disappear in Unpleasant samples
  (Atopobiaceae `r anc_un$Family |> filter(Family == "Atopobiaceae") |> with(paste0(fmt(mean_rel_abund_Normal, 1), "% vs ", fmt(mean_rel_abund_Unpleasant, 1), "%"))`).
* **q < 0.05 but not robust:** `r knitr::combine_words(nf(anc_un, "Family"))`.

##### Genus

```{r ancom-odor-un-genus}
anc_tbl(anc_un, "Genus", "fecal_odor", tab_no = "20e", g = c("Normal", "Unpleasant"))
```

```{r fig-top5-odor-un-genus, fig.cap = "Figure 14e. Five lowest-p taxa at Genus level (ANCOM-BC2), Unpleasant vs Normal."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_fecal_odor_U_vs_Normal_genus.png"))
```

* **Robust, higher in Unpleasant:** `r rob(anc_un, "Genus")`.
* **Robust, higher in Normal:** `r rob(anc_un, "Genus", up = FALSE)`;
  `r anc_un$Genus |> filter(Genus == "Leptogranulimonas") |> with(paste0(fmt(mean_rel_abund_Normal, 1), "% vs ", fmt(mean_rel_abund_Unpleasant, 1), "%"))`.
* **q < 0.05 but not robust:** `r knitr::combine_words(paste0("*", nf(anc_un, "Genus"), "*"))`.
  These include the abundant *Allobaculum* (`r anc_un$Genus |> filter(Genus == "Allobaculum") |> with(paste0(fmt(mean_rel_abund_Normal, 1), "% vs ", fmt(mean_rel_abund_Unpleasant, 1), "%"))`),
  whose decrease fails the sensitivity analysis.

##### Species

```{r ancom-odor-un-species}
anc_tbl(anc_un, "Species", "fecal_odor", tab_no = "20f", g = c("Normal", "Unpleasant"))
```

```{r fig-top5-odor-un-species, fig.cap = "Figure 14f. Five lowest-p taxa at Species level (ANCOM-BC2), Unpleasant vs Normal."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_fecal_odor_U_vs_Normal_species.png"))
```

* **Robust, higher in Unpleasant:** `r rob(anc_un, "Species")`.
* **Robust, higher in Normal:** `r rob(anc_un, "Species", up = FALSE)`.
* **q < 0.05 but not robust:** `r knitr::combine_words(paste0("*", nf(anc_un, "Species"), "*"))`.
* *Allobaculum* species move in opposite directions: *A. stercoricanis*
  rises (`r anc_un$Species |> filter(Species == "Allobaculum stercoricanis") |> with(paste0(fmt(mean_rel_abund_Normal, 1), "% vs ", fmt(mean_rel_abund_Unpleasant, 1), "%"))`), while *A.* sp910577085
  and *A. mucilyticum* fall.

**Unpleasant vs Normal overall.** This is the comparison that carries the
differences seen in Sections 7–9. Unpleasant samples have robustly more
Clostridia (Lachnospirales, Oscillospirales, Peptostreptococcales),
Peptococcia (UMGS1590) and Coriobacteriia (*Collinsella*), and robustly
less of two minor Coriobacteriales families (Atopobiaceae,
Eggerthellaceae) and *Leptogranulimonas*. The fall of the dominant
Bacillota_I / Erysipelotrichaceae / *Allobaculum* lineage is large and has
q < 0.05 from Phylum to Species, but fails the sensitivity analysis from
Phylum to Genus (only *Allobaculum* sp910577085 is robust), so it is
reported as probable rather than robust. Because a large drop of
one dominant group raises the relative share of all others, the many
"higher in Unpleasant" results should be read together with that drop.

  falls in Unpleasant samples.

**Unpleasant vs Moderately Unpleasant overall.** The pattern is the same
as Unpleasant vs Normal: Bacillota, Clostridia (Lachnospirales,
Peptostreptococcales), Peptococcia and Coriobacteriia (Coriobacteriaceae)
are robustly higher in Unpleasant, and Atopobiaceae is robustly lower.
Moderately Unpleasant samples therefore resemble Normal ones (Section
10.3.1), and Unpleasant is the only fecal_odor group that differs.

**fecal_odor overall.** Of the three comparisons, only those involving
Unpleasant show robust differences. This agrees with the separate
Unpleasant cluster in the PCoA (Figure 10c) and the large R² of fecal_odor
in PERMANOVA (Section 9.3).

# 11. Summary of the taxonomic analysis

```r
# Table 23 collects the results already shown, per comparison and in condition order:
#   alpha:      number of the six indices with Wilcoxon p < 0.05 (Section 6)
#   PERMANOVA:  R² and p_adj for all MAGs (Section 9)
#   ANCOM-BC2:  taxa with q < 0.05 and robust taxa, summed over Phylum to Species (Section 10)
sum(anc_g$Summary$Significant_q05); sum(anc_g$Summary$Also_pass_sensitivity)   # e.g. gender
```

```{r summary-tab}
rob_n <- function(a) sum(a$Summary$Also_pass_sensitivity)
q_n   <- function(a) sum(a$Summary$Significant_q05)
alpha_n <- function(g1, g2) atest |> filter(group1 == g1, group2 == g2, p < 0.05) |> nrow()
perm_all <- function(x) x |> filter(Level == "All features")
sm <- tibble(
  Condition  = c("gender", "fecal_color", "fecal_odor", "fecal_odor", "fecal_odor", "fecal_odor"),
  Comparison = c("male vs female", "Abnormally Dark vs Normal", "all three groups",
                 "Moderately Unpleasant vs Normal", "Unpleasant vs Normal",
                 "Unpleasant vs Moderately Unpleasant"),
  `Alpha indices p < 0.05` = c(alpha_n("female", "male"), alpha_n("Normal", "Abnormally Dark"), NA,
                               alpha_n("Normal", "Moderately Unpleasant"), alpha_n("Normal", "Unpleasant"),
                               alpha_n("Moderately Unpleasant", "Unpleasant")),
  `PERMANOVA R² all MAGs (%)` = c(fmt(100 * perm_all(pg)$R2, 1), fmt(100 * perm_all(pc9)$R2, 1),
                                 fmt(100 * perm_all(po9)$R2, 1), NA, NA, NA),
  `PERMANOVA p_adj` = c(p4(perm_all(pg)$p_adj), p4(perm_all(pc9)$p_adj), p4(perm_all(po9)$p_adj), NA, NA, NA),
  `ANCOM-BC2 q < 0.05` = c(q_n(anc_g), q_n(anc_c), NA, q_n(anc_mn), q_n(anc_un), q_n(anc_um)),
  `ANCOM-BC2 robust` = c(rob_n(anc_g), rob_n(anc_c), NA, rob_n(anc_mn), rob_n(anc_un), rob_n(anc_um)))
options(knitr.kable.NA = "-")
ctab(sm, caption = "Table 23. Overview of the taxonomic results by condition. Alpha: number of the six indices with nominal Wilcoxon p < 0.05; ANCOM-BC2: taxa summed over Phylum to Species.")
```

**Community.** The `r nrow(flt)` bacterial MAGs are dominated by
Bacillota_I (Erysipelotrichaceae, mainly *Allobaculum*), Bacillota
(Lachnospiraceae, Peptococcaceae) and Actinomycetota (*Collinsella*,
*Bifidobacterium*). Library size does not differ between groups in any
condition (Section 4), and all rarefaction curves saturate far below the
rarefaction depth (Section 5). Table 23 summarises the tests for each
condition, in the same order as the rest of the tutorial.

1. **gender.** No analysis detects a difference: alpha diversity, PCoA,
   PERMANOVA (R² `r fmt(100 * perm_all(pg)$R2, 1)`%, p_adj
   `r p4(perm_all(pg)$p_adj)`) and ANCOM-BC2 (no taxon with q < 0.05) all
   agree that female and male dogs carry similar communities.
2. **fecal_color.** Composition differs (R² `r fmt(100 * perm_all(pc9)$R2, 1)`%),
   but Abnormally Dark samples are also more variable (PERMDISP
   significant), and only Oscillospirales is robustly different in
   ANCOM-BC2. The difference comes from the
   `r sum(design$fecal_odor == "Unpleasant")` Abnormally Dark samples that
   are also Unpleasant (`r nrow(low_b1)` of them with less than 25%
   Bacillota_I); the other Abnormally Dark samples resemble Normal ones.
3. **fecal_odor.** The strongest effect (R² `r fmt(100 * perm_all(po9)$R2, 1)`%).
   Unpleasant samples form a separate PCoA cluster and differ from both
   Normal (`r rob_n(anc_un)` robust taxa) and Moderately Unpleasant
   (`r rob_n(anc_um)`): more Clostridia (Lachnospiraceae,
   Peptostreptococcaceae), Peptococcia (UMGS1590) and Coriobacteriaceae
   (*Collinsella*), less Atopobiaceae, and a large but non-robust fall of
   Bacillota_I / *Allobaculum*. They also have slightly fewer MAGs and less
   low-abundance rarity. Moderately Unpleasant samples do not differ from
   Normal (no robust taxon).

**Points to keep in mind.** fecal_color and fecal_odor overlap (every
Unpleasant sample is Abnormally Dark; Table 2), so their effects cannot
be separated in these samples, and the main signal is best described as
one group of nine Unpleasant, Abnormally Dark samples. Abundances are
estimated reads of non-dereplicated MAGs (Section 3), alpha-diversity
p-values are not adjusted, and the compositional shift after the fall of
Bacillota_I raises the relative share of other taxa.

---

# 12. Functional analysis (COG, EC, Pfam, KEGG KO, KEGG Module, KEGG Pathway)

The six functional groups (Section 1.5) are analysed with the same steps
as the taxonomy, in the order COG, EC, Pfam, KEGG KO, KEGG Module and KEGG
Pathway, and within each group in the order gender, fecal_color and
fecal_odor.

## 12.1 Functional alpha diversity

```r
ps_cog <- readRDS("phyloseq/ps_function.rds")$COG          # one phyloseq object per group
alpha  <- ps_cog |>
  ps_calc_richness(rank = "unique", index = "observed", varname = "Observed") |>
  ps_calc_diversity(rank = "unique", index = "shannon", varname = "Shannon") |>
  samdat_tbl()
wilcox.test(Shannon ~ gender, data = alpha, exact = FALSE)
```

Functional alpha diversity uses the same six indices as Section 6, with
functional terms (COGs, EC numbers, Pfam families, KOs, modules or
pathways) in place of MAGs, computed on the filtered functional tables
without rarefying. Here **richness** is the number of distinct functions
detected, **Shannon, Simpson and Pielou** describe how evenly the gene
abundance is spread over those functions, and **low-abundance rarity** is
the share of abundance carried by functions below 0.2%.

Each figure has one panel per index, one box per group and one point per
sample, with the two-sided nominal Wilcoxon p (brackets for the three
fecal_odor pairs).

### 12.1.1 COG


```r
a <- alpha_values(ps_function$COG)                       # six indices, not rarefied
alpha_tests(a, "gender"); alpha_tests(a, "fecal_color"); alpha_tests(a, "fecal_odor")   # Wilcoxon per pair
```

```{r fig-falpha-cog-gender, fig.cap = "Figure 16a. Functional alpha diversity of COG by gender."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "alpha_diversity_COG_gender.png"))
```

```{r fig-falpha-cog-fecal_color, fig.cap = "Figure 16b. Functional alpha diversity of COG by fecal_color."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "alpha_diversity_COG_fecal_color.png"))
```

```{r fig-falpha-cog-fecal_odor, fig.cap = "Figure 16c. Functional alpha diversity of COG by fecal_odor."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "alpha_diversity_COG_fecal_odor.png"))
```

* **gender (Figure 16a).** No index differs (p ≥ 0.68).
* **fecal_color (Figure 16b).** Richness does not differ (Observed and
  Chao1 p = 0.49), but Shannon (p = 0.015), Simpson (p = 0.017), Pielou
  (p = 0.04) and low-abundance rarity (p = 0.0026) are all higher in
  Abnormally Dark samples.
* **fecal_odor (Figure 16c).** The same four indices are higher in
  Unpleasant than in Normal (p = 0.00014–0.0033) and than in Moderately
  Unpleasant (p = 0.0009–0.0081); Normal and Moderately Unpleasant do not
  differ (p ≥ 0.64), and richness does not differ in any pair (p ≥ 0.74).

### 12.1.7 Summary of functional alpha diversity

Gender has no effect on functional alpha diversity in any group. For
fecal_color and fecal_odor, the number of functions never differs; the
differences are in how abundance is spread over them, and they come from
the Unpleasant (Abnormally Dark) samples. Against Normal and Moderately
Unpleasant samples, these have higher low-abundance rarity for COG and EC
(for Pfam only against Normal) and more even COG profiles, but less diverse KEGG Module and KEGG
Pathway profiles. KEGG KO shows no difference. All p-values are nominal.

## 12.2 Functional beta diversity

```r

  dist_calc("bray") |> ord_calc(method = "PCoA") |>
  ord_plot(colour = "gender")
```

Functional beta diversity compares the functional profiles of the samples:
Bray-Curtis dissimilarity on the relative abundance of all functional
terms in a group, ordinated by PCoA, drawn as in Section 8 (one point per

gender (a), fecal_color (b) and fecal_odor (c).

### 12.2.7 Summary of functional beta diversity

All six groups show the same structure as the MAG taxonomy (Section 8),
with MDS1 explaining 59.5-70.9% of the variation:

1. **gender.** Female and male samples are intermixed and their hulls
   largely overlap in every group.
2. **fecal_color.** Normal samples all fall in the right-hand cluster of
   MDS1; Abnormally Dark samples spread across both clusters, with S2, S3,
   S4, S6 and S7 among the Normal samples and the rest on the left.
3. **fecal_odor.** The nine Unpleasant samples (S1, S8, S9, S11, S13, S14,
   S15, S17, S29) form a separate cluster on the left of MDS1 in every
   group, whose hull does not touch the others; Normal and Moderately
   Unpleasant samples are intermixed.

The functional profiles therefore follow the taxonomic shift: the
Unpleasant samples differ in both community composition and functional
potential, while gender has no visible effect.

## 12.3 Functional PERMANOVA

```r
d <- ps_cog |> tax_transform("compositional", rank = "unique") |> dist_calc("bray")
d |> dist_permanova(variables = "gender", n_perms = 9999, seed = 2026) |> perm_get()  # PERMANOVA
d |> dist_bdisp(variables = "gender") |> bdisp_get()                                  # PERMDISP
```

PERMANOVA and PERMDISP are run as in Section 9 (Bray-Curtis, 9,999
permutations), once per functional group on all its features; p-values
are BH-adjusted across the six groups (p_adj). Each table has one row per
group: number of features, R², PERMANOVA p and p_adj, and PERMDISP p and
p_adj.

```{r fperm}
fperm <- read_csv(fun_perm_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = c("COG", "EC", "Pfam", "KEGG_KO", "KEGG_Module", "KEGG_Pathway"))) |>
  arrange(Group)
fperm_kable <- function(cn, tab) fperm |> filter(Condition == cn) |>
  transmute(Group = gsub("_", " ", Group), Features = fmt(Features), `R² (%)` = fmt(100 * R2, 2),
            p = pq(p), p_adj = pq(p_adj), `PERMDISP p` = pq(PERMDISP_p), `PERMDISP p_adj` = pq(PERMDISP_p_adj)) |>
  ctab(caption = sprintf("Table %s. Functional PERMANOVA and PERMDISP by %s (Bray-Curtis, 9,999 permutations; p_adj = BH across groups)", tab, cn))
fr <- function(cn) fperm |> filter(Condition == cn) |>
  with(paste0(fmt(100 * min(R2), 2), "% to ", fmt(100 * max(R2), 2), "%"))
fpd <- function(cn, sig = TRUE) fperm |> filter(Condition == cn, (PERMDISP_p_adj < 0.05) == sig) |>
  pull(Group) |> as.character() |> gsub(pattern = "_", replacement = " ") |> knitr::combine_words()
```

### 12.3.1 gender


```r
for (g in names(ps_function)) {                    # COG, EC, Pfam, KEGG KO, Module, Pathway
  d <- ps_function[[g]] |> tax_transform("compositional", rank = "unique") |> dist_calc("bray")
  print(d |> dist_permanova(variables = "gender", n_perms = 9999, seed = 2026) |> perm_get())
  print(d |> dist_bdisp(variables = "gender", method = "centroid") |> bdisp_get())
}
# p_adj = p.adjust(p, "BH") across the six groups
```

```{r fperm-gender}
fperm_kable("gender", "24a")
```

Gender explains only `r fr("gender")` of the functional variation, and
neither PERMANOVA (p_adj ≥ `r p4(min(fperm$p_adj[fperm$Condition == "gender"]))`)
nor PERMDISP is significant in any group.

### 12.3.2 fecal_color


```r
for (g in names(ps_function)) {                    # COG, EC, Pfam, KEGG KO, Module, Pathway
  d <- ps_function[[g]] |> tax_transform("compositional", rank = "unique") |> dist_calc("bray")
  print(d |> dist_permanova(variables = "fecal_color", n_perms = 9999, seed = 2026) |> perm_get())
  print(d |> dist_bdisp(variables = "fecal_color", method = "centroid") |> bdisp_get())
}
# p_adj = p.adjust(p, "BH") across the six groups
```

```{r fperm-color}

```

fecal_color explains `r fr("fecal_color")` of the variation and is
significant in every group (p_adj ≤ `r p4(max(fperm$p_adj[fperm$Condition == "fecal_color"]))`).
PERMDISP is also significant for `r fpd("fecal_color")`, where Abnormally
Dark samples are more spread out (Figures 22b–27b); only for
`r fpd("fecal_color", FALSE)` is the result a pure shift of the centroid.

variation (p = 0.0001 in every group). PERMDISP is significant for
`r fpd("fecal_odor")`, but not for `r fpd("fecal_odor", FALSE)`, where the
large R² therefore reflects a genuine difference in functional
composition, matching the separate Unpleasant cluster in Figures 22c–27c.

### 12.3.4 Summary of functional PERMANOVA

The functional results mirror the taxonomic ones (Section 9) at slightly
lower R²: gender has no effect (about 2%), fecal_color a moderate effect
(about 20%) that partly reflects the larger spread of Abnormally Dark
samples, and fecal_odor the strongest effect (about 50%), carried by the
Unpleasant samples. KEGG Pathway gives the highest R² for both faecal
conditions.

## 12.4 Functional differential abundance (ANCOM-BC2)

```r
res <- ANCOMBC::ancombc2(data = ps_cog, fix_formula = "gender",
                         p_adj_method = "holm", prv_cut = 0.10, pseudo_sens = TRUE)
```

ANCOM-BC2 is run as in Section 10, once per functional group and
comparison, with q-values Holm-adjusted over the features of each group.
For KEGG KO, COG, EC and Pfam the sampling bias is estimated from the
group's own features; for KEGG Module and KEGG Pathway it is estimated
from the KEGG KO features. Features that the primary fit cannot estimate
are refitted with a pseudo-count of 1 (marked *pseudo 1* in the figures).
A feature is **robust** when q < 0.05 and it passes the sensitivity
analysis. Each group has a table of the ten lowest-p features and a
figure of the five lowest-p features, shown regardless of significance.

```{r fanc-fun}
fanc_tbl <- function(a, r, cn, n = 10, tab_no, g = conditions[[cn]][1:2]) {
  d <- a[[r]] |> arrange(p) |> slice_head(n = n)
  bind_cols(tibble(Feature = d$feature, Name = d$description), feat_cols(d, g)) |>
    ctab(sprintf("Table %s. ANCOM-BC2, %s, %s vs %s (%s features; ten lowest p). Present = samples with reads, %s/%s.",
                            tab_no, gsub("_", " ", r), g[2], g[1], fmt(nrow(a[[r]])), g[1], g[2]))
}
fanc_sum <- function(a, tab, caption) a$Summary |>
  mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = c("COG", "EC", "Pfam", "KEGG_KO", "KEGG_Module", "KEGG_Pathway"))) |>
  arrange(Group) |>
  mutate(Group = gsub("_", " ", Group)) |>
  sum_cols("Group") |>
  ctab(sprintf("Table %s. %s", tab, caption))
fanc_txt <- function(a, r, g = NULL) {
  x <- a[[r]]
  rb <- x |> filter(significant) |> arrange(q)
  nr <- x |> filter(q < 0.05, !significant) |> arrange(q)
  lst <- function(d, k = 5) paste0(paste0(head(d$feature, k), " (", head(d$description, k), "; LFC ",
                                          formatC(head(d$lfc, k), format = "f", digits = 2), ")", collapse = "; "),
                                   if (nrow(d) > k) paste0("; and ", nrow(d) - k, " more") else "")
  if (nrow(rb) > 0) {
    up <- rb |> filter(lfc > 0); dn <- rb |> filter(lfc < 0)
    return(paste0("**", nrow(rb), " robust features** (", nrow(dn), " higher in ", g[1], ", ", nrow(up),
                  " higher in ", g[2], "; ", nrow(nr), " more with q < 0.05 fail the sensitivity analysis). ",
                  if (nrow(dn) > 0) paste0("Lowest q, higher in ", g[1], ": ", lst(dn), ". ") else "",
                  if (nrow(up) > 0) paste0("Lowest q, higher in ", g[2], ": ", lst(up), ".") else ""))
  }
  if (nrow(nr) == 0) return(paste0("**No robust feature.** No feature reaches q < 0.05; the lowest is ",
                                   x$feature[which.min(x$q)], " (", x$description[which.min(x$q)], "; q = ", p4(min(x$q)), ")."))
  paste0("**No robust feature.** ", nrow(nr), ifelse(nrow(nr) == 1, " feature reaches", " features reach"),
         " q < 0.05 but fail", ifelse(nrow(nr) == 1, "s", ""), " the sensitivity analysis: ", lst(nr), ".")
}
```

**Unpleasant vs Normal overall.** Many functions that are common in
Normal samples are much lower or absent in Unpleasant samples, which is why most robust
features (`r fu_dn` of `r fu_rob`) are higher in Normal. These include
RNA repair (RNA 2',3'-cyclic phosphodiesterase: COG1514, EC 3.1.4.58,
K01975, Pfam LigT_PEase), fructan degradation (fructan beta-fructosidase:
EC 3.2.1.80, K03332), toxin-antitoxin and CRISPR genes (K21493, K18828,
K19046), glutathione and cysteine biosynthesis (M00118, M00338) and
aromatic-compound degradation pathways (styrene, chlorocyclohexane and
toluene degradation). The few functions higher in Unpleasant include
opine dehydrogenase (EC 1.5.1.28), molybdenum cofactor
cytidylyltransferase (EC 2.7.7.76) and tryptophan-to-kynurenine
metabolism (M00038). The same enzyme often appears in several groups,
and the boxplots show little overlap between the two groups, so these results
follow the taxonomic shift of the Unpleasant samples (Section 10.3.2).

```r
ps_ab <- ps_function$COG |>
  ps_filter(fecal_odor %in% c("Moderately Unpleasant", "Unpleasant")) |>                       # only the two groups compared
  ps_mutate(fecal_odor = factor(fecal_odor, levels = c("Moderately Unpleasant", "Unpleasant")))      # Moderately Unpleasant = reference
res <- ANCOMBC::ancombc2(data = ps_ab, tax_level = NULL, fix_formula = "fecal_odor",
                         p_adj_method = "holm", prv_cut = 0.10, pseudo_sens = TRUE)
res$res   # lfc_, p_, q_ and passed_ss_ columns: Unpleasant vs Moderately Unpleasant
# script: run_ancombc2_safe(ps_function$COG, "COG", contrasts$fecal_odor__Unpleasant_vs_Moderately_Unpleasant);
#         KEGG Module / Pathway use bias_ps = ps_function$KEGG_KO
```

```{r fanc-odor-um-summary}
fa_um <- anc_read(fun_ancom_xlsx[["odor_U_MU"]])
fanc_sum(fa_um, "33", "Functional ANCOM-BC2 summary, Unpleasant vs Moderately Unpleasant (results/function/ancombc2_results_by_group_fecal_odor_Unpleasant_vs_Moderately_Unpleasant.xlsx, sheet 'Summary')")
fm_rob <- sum(fa_um$Summary$Also_pass_sensitivity)
fm_dn  <- sum(fa_um$Summary$Higher_in_Moderately_Unpleasant)
```

This comparison uses the `r fa_um$Run_status$Samples[1]` Moderately
Unpleasant and Unpleasant samples. `r fmt(sum(fa_um$Summary$Significant_q05))`
features reach q < 0.05 and **`r fm_rob` are robust**, `r fm_dn` of them
higher in Moderately Unpleasant and `r fm_rob - fm_dn` higher in
Unpleasant (Table 33). Fewer features are robust than against Normal
(`r fu_rob`), as this comparison has fewer samples (17 vs 22).

**Unpleasant vs Moderately Unpleasant overall.** The robust features are
largely the same as against Normal (Section 12.4.3.2) and point in the
same direction: RNA 2',3'-cyclic phosphodiesterase (COG1514, EC 3.1.4.58,
K01975, Pfam LigT_PEase), the toxin YxiD (K21493), CRISPR Cascade
subunits (K19046, K19124, K19123; Pfam CRISPR_Cse2), carboxylesterase
(EC 3.1.1.1) and the chlorocyclohexane, styrene and toluene degradation
pathways are all lower in Unpleasant samples. Moderately Unpleasant
samples therefore share the functional profile of Normal samples.

### 12.4.4 Summary of functional differential abundance

1. **gender.** No function differs robustly in any group.
2. **fecal_color.** No function differs robustly; the q < 0.05 results
   (mostly higher in Abnormally Dark) come from the Unpleasant subset of
   Abnormally Dark samples.
3. **fecal_odor.** Moderately Unpleasant does not differ from Normal.
   Unpleasant differs robustly from both Normal (`r fu_rob` features) and
   Moderately Unpleasant (`r fm_rob`), mostly through functions that are
   lower in Unpleasant samples, such as RNA repair, CRISPR, toxin and
   aromatic-compound degradation genes.

As in the taxonomic analysis, the functional differences belong to the
nine Unpleasant (and Abnormally Dark) samples.

## 12.5 Summary of the functional analysis

The six functional groups (COG, EC, Pfam, KEGG KO, KEGG Module, KEGG
Pathway) give a consistent picture that mirrors the taxonomy (Section 11):

1. **gender.** No effect in any analysis: functional alpha diversity,
   PCoA, PERMANOVA (R² 1.37–2.01%) and ANCOM-BC2 (no robust feature).
2. **fecal_color.** Functional composition differs (R² 19.19–25.17%), but
   Abnormally Dark samples are also more variable and no feature is
   robust in ANCOM-BC2; the signal comes from the Abnormally Dark samples
   that are also Unpleasant.
3. **fecal_odor.** The strongest effect (R² 47.63–56.28%). Unpleasant
   samples form a separate cluster in every group, have higher
   low-abundance rarity for COG and EC (and Pfam, against Normal) and less
   diverse KEGG Module and Pathway profiles, and differ robustly from Normal (`r fu_rob`
   features) and Moderately Unpleasant (`r fm_rob`), mostly through
   functions that are lower in Unpleasant samples, such as RNA repair,
   CRISPR, toxin-antitoxin and aromatic-compound degradation genes.
   Moderately Unpleasant samples do not differ from Normal.

The functional potential therefore changes together with the community:
the nine Unpleasant, Abnormally Dark samples differ in both which bacteria
are present and which functions they carry. As for the taxonomy, these are
estimated gene abundances from assembled contigs, the alpha-diversity
p-values are nominal, and the overlap of fecal_color and fecal_odor
(Table 2) means their effects cannot be separated.

# 13. Tools and libraries

| Tool | Version / source | Role |
|---|---|---|
| nf-core/mag [1, 2] | 5.5.0 (Nextflow [7], nf-core [8]) | upstream processing |
| fastp [9], Bowtie2 [10] | 1.0.1; 2.4.2 (nf-core/mag 5.5.0 containers) | read QC; PhiX and host removal |
| MEGAHIT [11], Prodigal [12] | 1.2.9; 2.6.3 | assembly; gene prediction |
| MetaBAT2 [13], MaxBin2 [14], MetaBinner [15] | 2.17; 2.2.7; 1.4.4 | binning |
| Tiara [16], DAS Tool [3] | 1.0.3; 1.1.7 | domain classification; bin refinement |
| CheckM2 [17] | 1.1.0 | MAG completeness and contamination |
| GTDB-Tk [4, 18], GTDB [5] | 2.7.2; GTDB release 232 (R11-RS232, April 2026) | MAG taxonomy |
| eggNOG-mapper [6, 22], eggNOG [21], DIAMOND [23] | eggNOG-mapper v2 (2.1.x; exact version printed by `1_prepare.sh`), eggNOG 5.0 | functional annotation |
| COG [24], ENZYME [25], Pfam [26], KEGG [27] | downloaded by steps 4 and 6 | term filtering and names |
| phyloseq [28] | Bioconductor | data handling |
| microViz [29] | r-universe | aggregation, diversity, ordination, PERMANOVA, bar plots |
| microbiome [30] | Bioconductor | evenness, rarity |
| vegan [31] | CRAN | rarefaction, adonis2, betadisper |
| ANCOMBC [32] | Bioconductor | ANCOM-BC2 |
